planting.note: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in part shade beneath deciduous trees; seed can also be fall-sown for natural cold-moist stratification. Spreads slowly by creeping rhizomes to form a quiet, low groundcover layer in dry shade where few other natives thrive.

directions: Licorice bedstraw is a rhizomatous woodland perennial of the bedstraw family found scattered through Ozark upland and lowland forests from Missouri south into Arkansas, where it forms loose, sprawling clumps of whorled leaves that smell faintly of licorice when crushed. Plant divisions or fall-sown seed in average to dry, well-drained soil in part shade beneath deciduous canopy; established plants spread slowly by creeping rhizomes and light self-seeding. Tiny greenish-yellow flowers appear from May into July and are followed by small bur-like fruits dispersed by ants. It is an easy, low-maintenance choice for dry woodland shade where showier wildflowers often struggle.

planting.note: Fall-sow seed outdoors to allow natural cold-moist stratification over winter, or set out nursery divisions in spring; plant in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in part shade along a shaded slope, ravine, or woodland edge. Established colonies also spread by rooting at the stem nodes.

directions: Largeflower valerian is a clump-forming woodland perennial of rich, mesic ravines and streamside forests across the Interior Highlands, with documented populations in the Missouri Ozarks as well as the Appalachian and Interior Low Plateau region. Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in part shade; it spreads modestly by rooting at the stem nodes once established. From May into June it sends up loose, rounded heads of pale pink, long-tubed flowers above broad, pinnately divided leaves, a striking combination among spring woodland wildflowers. It pairs well with ferns and sedges in a shaded native garden and is offered by several specialty native plant nurseries as plugs or potted stock.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant potted divisions or plugs in spring, spacing 12-18 inches apart, in average to moist soil anywhere from full sun to part shade; the clump fills in within two growing seasons. Useful as a transitional sedge between sunny borders and shaded woodland plantings.

directions: Bush's sedge is a clump-forming native sedge of moist meadows, woodland edges, and open bottomland forest across the eastern and central United States, including the Ozark region of Missouri and Arkansas. It grows easily in average to moist soil from full sun into part shade, making it a versatile transition plant between sunny borders and shaded woodland plantings. Reddish-brown, burr-like seed spikes appear on separate flowering culms in May and June above a fine-textured, arching clump of foliage. It is listed as a regional native by the Grow Native! program of the Missouri Prairie Foundation and sold by specialty native plant nurseries as plugs or potted divisions.

planting.note: Direct sow seed in fall for natural cold-moist stratification, or set out potted plants in spring, in moist to average soil under full woodland canopy. One of the few ornamental grasses that genuinely thrives in deep shade.

directions: Nodding fescue is a cool-season bunchgrass of mesic deciduous forests throughout the Ozark-Ouachita Highlands and eastern United States, notable for tolerating more shade than almost any other native grass. Fine green leaf blades form a low tuft beneath slender flowering stems that rise 2 to 3 feet and arch over at the tip, giving the airy, drooping seedhead that gives the species its common name. Direct sow seed in fall for natural cold stratification, or set out potted plants in spring, in moist to average, well-drained soil under full woodland canopy. It is widely offered by Midwestern native seed and plug nurseries as a true deep-shade substitute for ornamental fescues.

planting.note: Direct sow seed in fall for natural cold-moist stratification, or plant plugs in spring, in fertile loamy to clay soil in part to full shade beneath mature trees. Softer and more shade-tolerant than the related Virginia wildrye (Elymus virginicus).

directions: Silky wild rye is a cool-season woodland bunchgrass native to rich deciduous forests across the eastern and central United States, including Ozark bottomland and upland woods, distinguished from the related Virginia wildrye by its softer, more delicate habit and the fine silky hairs covering the upper leaf surfaces. Direct sow seed in fall for cold-moist stratification, or plant plugs in spring, in fertile, loamy to clay soil in part to full shade beneath mature trees. Slender, nodding seed heads with long, bristly awns appear from June into August atop arching stems, providing texture and wildlife food value through fall and winter. It is an excellent companion grass for woodland wildflower plantings and is sold directly by Prairie Moon Nursery and other regional native plant growers.
